The answer is: (a fictional Inuit village on the coast of Greenland) went out hunting. One shot an arrow through the shoulder of a caribou, but did not kill it. The other shot at a seal, but missed. Both men lost their quarry and went to bed. In the morning, one man found the caribou dead, and the other man found the seal dead also. Both men took their prey to the village. Later, one man bragged to the other that he had killed the caribou, and the other man lied and said that he had killed the seal. Soon after, both men were arrested by the village elders and brought before the community council. The council decided that since both men had lied about their kills, neither would be allowed to hunt for three years. After serving their sentences, both men were allowed to hunt again.

Adaptation
The story is retold in the 1991 book Hunting Magic: An Inuit Kidney Book by Willie Martin, with illustrations by Diane Burns. The title is a play on words with a children's book about a kidney stone, as the Inuit language has no word for "kidney". The story is told as a lesson about honesty.

The answer is: a native tribe from northern Canada, came to our camp. They were friendly and unarmed, so we let them approach. They were eager to trade and brought many strange devices. One of these they called "medicine," and said it would cure all our ills. It was a small box with many compartments, and in each compartment there was a dried animal, bird, or fish.
"Now," said the men from Egulac, "you must not open this medicine box until you are in danger, and then only open one compartment at a time, and quickly close it, or you will anger the gods and they will take their medicine away from you."
We agreed, and for two days the box was an object of great interest and mystery. Finally, when we were all alone, I opened it. There was no question of angering the gods, for there were no gods. There was only the endless desert, and the thought of all those dried animals, birds, and fish.
So we ate, and we grew fat, and we sang, and we danced, and we grew fat. And when we grew thin again, we ate, and we grew fat, and we sang, and we danced, and we grew fat.

Analysis
This story is an example of the common theme of "magic medicine" found in many Native American oral traditions. The medicine box is a common motif in oral traditions of many Native American cultures. It is often accompanied by a warning not to open the box unless one is in great need, and then only to take out one item. If the container is opened carelessly, or if an item is not replaced after being used, dire consequences will follow.The story is also an example of Native American oral tradition being influenced by contact with European culture. The answer is: a native tribe from northern Canada, came to our camp. They were friendly and unassuming, and when they left they took with them two white men. When we woke up the next morning we found that our camp had been raided and that four of our people had been taken. We decided to follow the Egulacs to get our people back.
We traveled for two days and then we saw them. The Egulacs were camped on a small island in the middle of a large lake. We knew that we were outnumbered, but we also knew that we could not let the Egulacs keep our people. So we attacked.
During the battle I managed to kill one of the Egulac warriors, but I was wounded severely. When the smoke cleared we counted five Egulac warriors lying on the ground. We had won the battle, but at a great cost. We had lost three of our people and I was the only one who had been able to fight.
As we were gathering up the bodies of our people and the Egulacs, I heard a noise behind me. I turned around and saw a group of Egulacs coming over the hill. They had come back to bury their dead. I knew that if we left now we could escape, but I also knew that we could not leave the Egulacs unburied. So we stayed and helped them bury their people.
After the burial we packed up our things and left. As we were walking away I looked back and saw the Egulacs standing around the graves, singing a mournful song. I knew then that even though we had won the battle, we had lost something inside of us. From that day on we never raided the Egulac camps, and we never took their lives.

Adapted from "One Night Two Men From Egulac" by Tomson Highway, Ojibwe storyteller.

One of them, named Naum, was an experienced huntsman, the other, called Aviu, was a young man who was hunting for the first time. Naum told Aviu that he would soon be home, and then he fell asleep in the canoe. Aviu rowed and rowed, and soon he was far out at sea. He awoke Naum, and they continued rowing. Suddenly, a huge wave splashed over the canoe, and it was carried out to sea. Naum and Aviu rowed and rowed, but they could not get back to land. They were soon far out at sea, and they could see no land.

They had no food, and they began to pray to the gods. The sun began to rise, and it grew light. Then they saw a big rock, and they rowed to it. They climbed up on the rock, and they saw another rock, and between the two rocks they saw a little piece of driftwood. On the driftwood sat a seal, and the two men took it for a seal. They skinned it, and they ate it, and they were soon refreshed. Then they prayed to the gods, and the gods heard their prayer, and they were saved.

They rowed back to their village, and they were welcomed by the women and the children. Naum scolded Aviu, and Aviu was sorry. But Naum forgave him, and they were friends again. From that time on Aviu was a good huntsman, and he helped Naum in all things.

This is a traditional Inuit story. It was recorded by Peary in 1892.

The story is a Canadian urban legend which has been told since at least the 1950s. For example, it is sometimes claimed that the two men were actually a white man and a Native American man, or that they were lovers. It is also often claimed that the woman was a 14-year-old girl.The story was told by Peter Stumpp in the 1950s, and was recorded by folklorist Richard Dorson in 1958.

Analysis
This legend is an example of a cautionary tale. The specific caution is not clear, as there are several variations on the story. One possible interpretation is that the tale is a warning against drinking to excess. Another is that the tale is a warning about the dangers of being alone with a potentially violent man. A 1998 analysis of the story by a Canadian broadcaster suggested that the story originated with frontier settlers and was a warning about the dangers of encountering a lone Native American man.

It is similar to the American urban legend "The Legend of the Piazza," and like that story, it is often expanded upon by adding details. For example, it is sometimes claimed that the two men were actually a white man and a Native American man, or that they were lovers. It is also sometimes claimed that the woman was a 14-year-old girl.The story was told by Peter Stumpp in the 1950s, and was recorded by folklorist Richard Dorson in 1958.

Analysis
This legend is an example of a cautionary tale. The specific caution is not clear, as there are several variations on the story. One possible interpretation is that the tale is a warning against drinking to excess. Another is that the tale is a warning about the dangers of being alone with a potentially violent man. A 1998 analysis of the story by a Canadian broadcaster suggested that the story originated with frontier settlers and was a warning about the dangers of encountering a lone Native American man.

Background
The story of "One Night Two Men from Egulac" is set in the time of the Mughal emperor Akbar. Two men from rival clans, Raja Puran and Raja Sohan, decided to end their generations-long feud and meet at a predetermined time and place. Egulac was a place on the banks of the Ganges where the two clans would hold their meetings. One night, as decided, the two men met. They were supposed to light a lamp at a certain hour to signal the end of the truce negotiations. However, both men being arrogant, each thought that the other would light the lamp, and so neither did. The night passed, and when the dawn broke, both men realized what a mistake they had made. By then, it was too late, as both men had been killed in the fight that ensued. It is also believed that the two men were in love with the same woman, who was either a begum or a gordon.

History
In 1871, two men from Egulac, John Wilson and Charles Vincent, attempted to abduct Ada Chelsey, a white woman, from her home in New Westminster, British Columbia. Chelsey was the wife of Arthur Stanley Chelsey, a man of mixed ancestry who was considered white by the dominant culture. Their home was next to the Chelsey House Hotel, where Wilson and Vincent were guests. The two men were intoxicated and armed. They wrapped Ada in a sheet and carried her into the hotel, intending to take her to Egulac "for pleasure and for keeps." Ada Chelsey was able to free herself, draw her revolver, and shoot Wilson, wounding him severely. Vincent fled with her purse.The incident was widely reported in the newspapers and caused great outrage among the white settlers. Authorities were slow to act, and it was feared that vigilante action would result. Therefore, on November 15, 1871, the Governor of British Columbia, Arthur Balfour, issued a proclamation creating the "Royal Mounted Police Force" (later the Royal Canadian Mounted Police). The force was to maintain peace on the frontier by preventing illegal activities, such as whiskey trading, and by removing lawless elements, including "Indian fighters" such as Wilson and Vincent.

History
In 1871, two men from Egulac, John Wilson and Charles Vincent, attempted to abduct Ada Chelsey, a white woman, from her home in New Westminster, British Columbia. Chelsey was able to prevent the abduction and in the struggle that ensued, she was able to shoot and wound Vincent. Wilson escaped.The incident was widely reported in the newspapers and caused great alarm among the settlers. As a result, the colonial government of British Columbia took action. It was felt that the North-West Mounted Police, which had been formed in 1873, was too far away to provide effective police protection. Therefore, on October 12, 1874, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) was formed. The RCMP was charged with maintaining law and order in British Columbia.
The two men, Wilson and Vincent, were arrested and charged with kidnapping. At their trial, Chelsey was called as a witness. She recounted how the two men had attempted to drag her from her home and how she had fought them. Despite her brave actions, she was sued for damages by Vincent. The case was heard in December 1874 and Chelsey was ordered to pay Vincent $600. The incident with Chelsey was one of several factors which led to the formation of the RCMP.

The answer is: Since the poem was published in 1866, it has been supposed by some that it was written in reaction to the American Civil War. In the poem, two cowboys are waiting in a saloon for a third who has been delayed by business. When the third cowboy arrives, he reveals that the two now-empty beds reflect the futility of war, and the folly of violence.However, other sources suggest that Swinburne may not have realized the conflict was futile, and wished to voice his sympathy for the South. 
 Still others interpret the poem as an analogy for sexual conquest. The first two stanzas describe the speaker's desire for two women named Anne and Florence, who are together, and his frustration at being unable to possess them. In the final stanza, the speaker desires a third woman named Liloë, who represents both the speaker's desire and his desire for vengeance against Anne and Florence.

Some YouTube videos claim to detail the "True Story" behind the poem, claiming that Swinburne saw two criminals beaten by police, and went home and wrote the poem in rage and despair, unable to understand how such violence could be justified.

History
The North American egulac (also spelled 'egrolla') were a group of Algonquin speakers who belonged to the Ottawa branch of the Algonquian language family. Their traditions place them on the shores of what is now Lake Huron in the late 15th century. Around 1570, the holy spirit introduced the Egulac to an European chief named John Herman, who came from the lands east of the great Lake St. Lawrence. Herman was probably a member of the Huron people, and may have been a chief of the Wendat people. The Egulac adopted the Christian religion and the European language, thereby ceasing to be a unified tribal group. Many joined the Michel Sect of Christianity. The Turgot family was one of the finest singers and drummers and belonged to the church. Another Egulac chief, named Georges, was altogether more influenced by the Germans. The British captured and executed him in 1763 when trying to reassert British authority over the region.
The prophetic works refer to the missionary society of the Protestant Reformed Church of America and the Presbyterian Church (USA).
